threat_internal_label: people using deepfaked colleagues to steal (never shown on screen)
analog: Deepfake video-conference fraud against the Hong Kong office of a multinational engineering firm (later named as Arup), January 2024: HK$200 million (~US$25.6M) sent in 15 transfers
actors_note: The red is people's choices: fraudsters took public videos of real executives and chose to fake a meeting to steal money. The software is not the actor. On screen: a gray video grid where every face but one is hollow, a hand behind the curtain pressing 'play'. The employee is not the fool: he was suspicious, and the routing to the one person who could confirm was missing.
t0: the day of the fake video call, 'mid-January' 2024; exact date not published. Working assumption t0 = 2024-01-22 (police report Jan 29 minus the ~1 week the ordeal lasted); every t below depends on it and is marked where so.

sources.title: CNN: Finance worker pays out $25 million after video call with deepfake 'chief financial officer' (Feb 4, 2024) - initially suspected a phishing email about a 'secret transaction'; realised after checking with head office

Hong Kong Free Press: Multinational loses HK$200 million to deepfake video conference scam, Hong Kong police say (Feb 5, 2024) - police received the report Jan 29; 15 transfers to 5 local accounts; pre-recorded deepfakes built from public video

CNN Business: Arup revealed as victim of $25 million deepfake scam involving Hong Kong employee (May 16, 2024) - the ordeal lasted a week from first contact to the company looking into it; Arup notified police in January
Hong Kong Free Press: In first, Hong Kong police arrest 6 over finance scams involving deepfake technology (Aug 25, 2023) - face-swap used to defeat bank facial checks on loan applications

HKSAR Government, LCQ9: Combating frauds involving deepfake (Jun 26, 2024) - Anti-Deception Coordination Centre advice: verify with a phone call when asked to remit via video or audio; Scameter; Anti-Scam Helpline 18222
HKSAR Government: Police launch Anti-Deception Coordination Centre website (Apr 1, 2021)

Sumsub (identity-verification VENDOR): Global Deepfake Incidents Surge Tenfold from 2022 to 2023 (Nov 2023) - 10x globally; 1,740% North America, 1,530% APAC, 780% Europe; crypto+fintech 96% of cases. Vendor sells deepfake detection: bias flagged.

points.event: all 15 transfers (HK$200M) made before the employee checks with head office, ~1 week after first contact
points.notes: s3 says the ordeal lasted about a week; how the 15 transfers were spread inside that week was not found (some secondary sources say a single day; unconfirmed)

growth_context.notes: Background growth only, not this event's timeline: an identity-verification vendor reports detected deepfakes rose ~10x worldwide from 2022 to 2023 (APAC +1,530%). Vendor data from its own customers, sold alongside its detection product; not independent, not a population rate. Don't put on screen without that caveat. Hong Kong police first found deepfakes used in finance fraud in Aug 2023 (s4).

threat.notes: extent = share of the HK$200M sent. Endpoints only. The funds were not reported recovered.

fragments.had: the right suspicion: he first thought the 'secret transaction' email was phishing
fragments.notes: the fragment existed before the call; the fake meeting talked him out of it

fragments.who: the real CFO and head office in the UK
fragments.had: the truth: no such meeting, no such transaction
fragments.notes: one call to a known number would have connected f1 and f2; it happened ~1 week later

fragments.had: prior cases of deepfakes used in fraud (Aug 2023 arrests)
fragments.notes: Aug 25, 2023 is 150 days before the assumed t0

fragments.had: a scam hotline and the standard advice: verify a remittance request by phone
fragments.notes: website launched Apr 1, 2021 (1,026 days before the assumed t0); the centre itself is older (not verified). The 'verify with a phone call' wording is documented in Jun 2024 (s5); whether it was published in the same words before t0 was not checked

aggregation.notes: Derived from documented dates, not a measured distribution, all relative to the assumed t0 = Jan 22, 2024: p10 = employee checks with head office, ~1 week (t=7, s3), police report Jan 29 (s2); median = police go public with the method, Feb 2 briefing reported Feb 4-5 (t~11, s1/s2); p90 = the firm publicly confirms it was the victim so others can learn, May 16 (t=115, s3). Government written answer with formal advice Jun 26 (t=156, s5).

deploy.notes: Deployment here is the warning reaching other companies (police briefing). Nothing was deployed in time for this victim; the money had already gone.

ai_counterfactual.basis: Illustrative. The fraudsters used AI to fake faces; the counterfactual is the company using AI for routing, not for spotting fake faces. A payment assistant sees a first-time payee, 'secret' and urgency in the request (classic business-email-compromise signs) and automatically asks the real CFO, on a number already on file, to confirm before release: connecting f1 (suspicion) to f2 (the truth). That is a minutes-scale routing task inside the ~17.4 h 50% task horizon in RATES.md (METR entry), and cheap to run on every payment given RATES.md's ~40x/yr cost fall (Epoch). Assumed ~0.05 days (~1 h) versus ~7 days. A human still confirms or refuses the payment. No claim that detection of the deepfake itself would work.
ai_counterfactual.label: illustrative

gap_summary: The money was gone within about a week of one fake meeting; the one fragment that could stop it, a call to the real CFO, sat in the same company from day 0 and connected only after ~7 days.
